INTRODUCTION

Healthcare SC, LLC (Healthcare SC) owns and operates a polyurethane foam manufacturing facility (Facility) located at 1 Mlily Way in Winnsboro, South Carolina. The Facility began operations in December 2019. Healthcare SC produces slabstock polyurethane foam by chemically reacting polyether polyols, diisocyanates, and minor additives. The cured foam is then incorporated into foam mattresses. 

The manufacturing process utilizes Mondur TD Grade A (TD80) as a raw material, generically referred to as Toluene Diisocyanate (TDI). The Facility comprises eight (8) TDI storage tanks - three (3) tanks with a capacity of 4,500 gallons and five (5) tanks with a capacity of 6,628-gallons. The tanks are located indoors in two separate locations on the north end of the Facility. Additionally, up to eighty 55-gallon drums of TDI can be stored in the unloading operations building. TD80 contains 2,4-Toluene Diisocyanate (2,4-TDI, CAS # 584-84-9) and 2,6-Toluene Diisocyanate (2,6-TDI, CAS # 91-08-7), both of which are regulated toxic substances listed in Table 1 of 40 CFR 68. The threshold quantity (TQ) for these chemicals is 10,000 pounds (lbs). Due to the exceedance of the TQ, the Facility is required to have a Risk Management Plan (RMP) in accordance with 40 CFR 68. This RMP has been developed based on the worst-case scenarios for five processes at the Facility.  

Process 1 includes three (3) TDI storage tanks (each 4,500 gallons), and associated piping. The worst-case scenario in this process is a catastrophic failure of a storage tank with a full capacity of 4,500 gallons. These storage tanks are located indoors in a room on the northeast end of the building. The room itself provides containment in the event of an accidental release. Therefore, the liquid contents of a worst-case release from Process 1 would be contained within the building. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will n

ot extend beyond the property and will not affect any public receptors.  

Process 2 is the TDI unloading process (entitled TDI Unloading 1) outside the manufacturing building that delivers the material to the storage tanks mentioned in Process 1. TDI will be delivered by tanker trucks with an expected capacity of 6,000 gallons. However, the worst-case release scenario analysis has been performed conservatively by assuming that the entire contents of a 11,600-gallon tanker would be released. TDI released during unloading would flow to the north into an approximately three-foot tall concrete containment area. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will not extend beyond the property and will not affect any public receptors.

Process 3 includes the five (5) remaining TDI storage tanks and associated piping. These 6,628-gallon horizontal storage tanks are located indoors in an area on the northwest corner of the building, approximately 165 feet west of the Process 1 tank storage location. The Process 3 tank storage location is surrounded by three walls and a concrete berm for containment in the event of an accidental release. Therefore, a worst-case release of the entire 6,628 gallons from a single tank from Process 3 would be contained within the building. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will not extend beyond the property and will not affect any public receptors.  

Process 4 is the TDI unloading process (entitled TDI Unloading 2) located within the unloading operations building (located to the north of the manufacturing building) and delivers TDI to the Process 3 tank storage location. The unloading operation building is partially open enabling tankers to drive into the bay for unloading materials and proceeding through the opposite side once delivery is complete. TDI will be delivered by tanker trucks w

ith an expected capacity of 6,000 gallons. However, the worst-case release scenario analysis has been performed conservatively by assuming that the entire contents of a 11,600-gallon tanker would be released. TDI released during unloading would flow downgrade into a deep containment pit below the building. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will not extend beyond the property and will not affect any public receptors. 

Finally, Process 5 includes the storage of TDI in 55-gallon drums within the unloading operation building. The worst-case release of the contents from the largest, single vessel would be a 55-gallon uncontained release, as the building is partially open near the truck bays. The worst-case release scenario analysis performed in accordance with 40 CFR §68.25 indicates that the toxic endpoint will not extend beyond the property and will not affect any public receptors.  

The Facility has not had any reportable accidental releases. As mentioned above, the distance to the toxic endpoint associated with a worst-case release is less than the distance to any public receptor. Finally, Healthcare SC has coordinated with local emergency planning and response organizations. Therefore, per 40 CFR §68.10(f), the Facility meets the eligibility requirements for RMP Program 1 for each of the five (5) processes.

ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION

The company takes safety of employees and the surrounding public seriously; hence Healthcare SC has policies and procedures in place to prevent an accidental release. The Release Prevention Program is designed to ensure proper working order of the equipment, safe tank filling, and employee safety. Safety begins with proper training of all employees in the dangers and appropriate handling of the materials and equipment. This training will be conducted during on-boarding and annually at a minimum.   

Preventative maintenance and inspections are con

ducted to ensure proper working order of all equipment. Regular inspections are conducted on all tanks, piping, pumps, and manufacturing equipment to minimize the risk of failure or leaks. Delivery tankers are inspected before and after unloading the raw materials to ensure there are no spills or leaks. Healthcare SC has a policy to limit tank filling to 90% of tank capacity to prevent spillage from overfilling.  

EMERGENCY RESPONSE

The Facility qualifies for RMP Program 1 and has coordinated with local agencies to have the Facility included in the community emergency response plan. Further, the Facility is a non-responding stationary source, meaning that Healthcare SC personnel will not respond to a release of a regulated substance. Therefore, per 40 CFR §68.90(b), this RMP need not include the specific emergency response program requirements of 40 CFR §68.95. The Facility will follow the general emergency response procedures discussed below. 

In the unlikely event of a TDI release, employees are to pull the fire alarm, which will signal immediate evacuation of the building and shut down the manufacturing process. As the chemicals are located in the northern portion of the building, employees will move to the southern portion of the property, unless it is deemed unsafe due to the direction of the wind flow at the time. The Environmental Health and Safety Supervisor, who serves as the RMP Emergency Contact, will immediately notify Fairfield County Emergency Management Agency (the local emergency response agency) to assist in the coordination of the safest and quickest response to contain any release, minimizing exposure to emergency responders, employees, and the public.  

The Fairfield County Emergency Medical Service would transport any injured parties to the nearest hospital, as appropriate in responding to the medical needs of the patient. Once the scene is deemed safe, an emergency cleanup contractor will conduct the remediation and remove the hazardous w

aste. The Central Midlands Local Emergency Planning Commission (LEPC) and South Carolina State Emergency Response Commission (SERC) have both been notified in case response assistance is required from regional or state emergency resources. The Facility will continue to coordinate with the SERC, LEPC, and other response agencies to ensure preparedness in the event of an accidental release.

Healthcare SC realizes the concerns of utilizing TDI in the manufacturing process. The Data Safety Sheet (SDS) indicates TDI vapors are dangerous and can lead to breathing difficulties or death if inhaled. TDI should only be handled while wearing permeation-resistant protective gloves and clothing. Breathing of vapors, spray or dust should be avoided by wearing adequate respiratory protection, such as self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA). An emergency shower and eye wash station are located in the production area in case of exposure. 


WORST-CASE RELEASE SCENARIO ANALYSIS

EPAs ALOHA model was used to determine the range of exposure of dangerous concentrations in the event of a worst-case scenario for each of the five processes  tank storage in two locations, drum storage, and materials unloading in two locations. The first scenario is a catastrophic failure of a storage vessel in the smaller tank room containing Toluene Diisocyanate (TDI), the second scenario is a catastrophic failure of a tanker while unloading TDI, and the third scenario is a catastrophic failure of a TDI-storage vessel in a second indoor tank location. Additionally, the fourth scenario is a catastrophic tanker failure in the second raw material unloading area at the Facility, and lastly, the fifth worst-case scenario involves an uncontained release of a full 55-gallon drum of TDI onto concrete. The substance to be stored at the Facility is a mixture of 2,4-TDI (60-80% composition) and 2,6-TDI (10-30% composition). As a measure of caution, the model was run for both 2,4-TDI and 2,6-TDI. The distance to

the endpoints for 2,6-TDI were consistently further-reaching than for 2,4-TDI. In an effort of conservativeness, the results from 100% composition of 2,6-TDI have been included here. The following is a discussion on the assumptions and parameters input into the ALOHA model.

The location of the Facility is in Winnsboro, SC [34.33° N, 81.08° W], which is approximately 25 miles north of Columbia. The elevation at this point is 560 feet above sea level. Guidelines for atmospheric parameters are presented in 40 CFR §68.22. Per §68.22(c), the highest temperature recorded in the past three years at the location is to be used for modeling. Data from the National Climate Data Center indicates the highest temperature recorded in Winnsboro since June 1, 2022, was 103? . The temperature of the substance is assumed to be the same as air temperature. A wind speed of 1.5 m/s was used in accordance with §68.22(b). Partly cloudy skies with no temperature inversion is a climatologically sound assumption. The relative humidity was assumed to be 60% based on the average annual air temperature of 66? and dewpoint of 52? . The atmospheric stability class F was used in accordance with §68.22(b).
